deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 123 continues a set of German history notes, probably lecture or textbook excerpts, on Greek history in the age of Philip II of Macedon. It runs on from folio 122 (Phocion, the Phocian War, Thermopylae 346) and into the next folio (Chaeronea, Philip's murder in 336, Alexander). The hand is a regular Kurrent school or notebook hand. Blue-ink corrections ('Aeschines', 'Locrier') were added by a second hand or at a second pass. Nothing ties the content to Gauss's mathematical work, despite the bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816'.

Content, in order:
(1) After the dealings of Demosthenes and Aeschines (the 346 embassies and the Peace of Philocrates are implied), Philip expanded northward. He aimed to widen his kingdom's borders and conquer the Greek colonies on the Thracian coast.
(2) From 344 on he subdued several Thracian peoples, so that the Danube and the Adriatic became his borders.
(3) In 341 he besieged Perinthus and Byzantium with 30,000 men. The Athenians, roused by Demosthenes, aided the Perinthians, and in 340 Philip had to lift both sieges.
(4) The Locrians (of Amphissa) were outlawed for cultivating a consecrated piece of land. This is the Amphictyonic decree that opened the Fourth Sacred War.
(5) In 338 Philip seized Elatea. Athens and Thebes allied and fielded an army against him, leading to the battle of Chaeronea, which the next page continues.

No derivation exists to reconstruct.
errors: Historical chronology is shifted by about a year relative to the modern consensus. The siege of Perinthus and Byzantium is now dated 340-339 BC, not 341-340. The seizure of Elatea was late 339, not 338; only Chaeronea (August 338) falls in 338.
The Athenians mainly aided Byzantium. Perinthus was relieved chiefly with Persian help from the satraps. The text says Athens helped the Perinthians.
Calling the Danube and the Adriatic Philip's borders is a conventional exaggeration found in older handbooks.
The 30,000 figure follows Diodorus and is unproblematic as a source citation.

results.what: Narrative history notes on Philip II of Macedon: Thracian expansion, the sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium, the Amphissan (Fourth Sacred) War, Elatea, and the run-up to Chaeronea.
results.usually_credited_to: Standard classical sources (Diodorus XVI, Demosthenes, Plutarch) as transmitted in early-19th-century German school handbooks.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine history notes with no mathematical content. It is likely a student notebook and possibly not even in Gauss's hand. Nothing here bears on the history of mathematics.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Nach[?] ... Untersuchst[?]' is doubtful. The sense requires something like 'Nach Demosthenes und Aeschines Unterhandlungen' (negotiations). 'Untersuchst' is almost certainly a misreading.
Line 1: 'bereitete sich Philipp ... aus' should probably read 'breitete sich Philipp ... aus' (spread out), given the separable verb 'ausbreiten' completed by 'aus' on line 2.

The blue marginal word at upper right is 'Aeschines', replacing a struck-through word. It is keyed by '+' to the insertion 'und' after 'Demosthenes' in line 1. The struck word is not 'Aeschines' itself, so the '[-Aeschines-]' deletion in the transcription is likely wrong.
'Die Lorier' is corrected in blue to 'Locrier', meaning the Amphissan Locrians.
'entheiligten[?] Stück Landes' fits the sense of profaned sacred land (the Kirrhaean plain), so the reading is plausible.
